misconceptions.statement: The ancient Olympic Games were held in the city of Athens.
misconceptions.why: Athens is the best-known Greek city and hosted the first modern Games, so students link every Olympics to it.
misconceptions.fix: The ancient Games were held at Olympia, a sacred site in southern Greece, in honour of Zeus. Athens hosted only the first modern Games in 1896.

probe.question: Where were the ancient Olympic Games held?

misconceptions.root_belief: the most famous place is where everything happened

misconceptions.statement: The Olympic Games have been held without a break since ancient times.
misconceptions.why: Textbooks stress the long tradition, so students imagine one continuous line from ancient Greece to now.
misconceptions.fix: The ancient Games ended around 393 CE and were revived in 1896. Even the modern Games were cancelled in 1916, 1940 and 1944 because of world wars.

probe.question: Was any modern Olympics ever cancelled?
probe.wrong_answer: No, they are held every four years without fail

misconceptions.root_belief: old traditions have continued unbroken

misconceptions.statement: The Olympic Games are held every year.
misconceptions.why: Students see sports events like leagues and championships every year and assume the Olympics are the same.
misconceptions.fix: A Summer Olympics is held once every four years, and so is a Winter Olympics. Each is called an Olympiad cycle.

probe.question: After Tokyo 2020 (held in 2021), in which year was the next Summer Olympics held?

misconceptions.root_belief: regular events happen every year

misconceptions.statement: The Summer and Winter Olympics are held in the same year, one after the other.
misconceptions.why: Both are called Olympics, so students think they are two parts of one event.
misconceptions.fix: Since 1994 the Winter and Summer Games alternate, falling two years apart. For example, Winter 2022 was followed by Summer 2024.

probe.question: Paris hosted the Summer Games in 2024. In which year was the Winter Olympics held before it?

misconceptions.root_belief: things with the same name happen together

misconceptions.statement: Each coloured ring stands for one particular country that started the Olympics.
misconceptions.why: The coloured rings look like flag colours, so students read them as countries.
misconceptions.fix: The five interlocked rings stand for the five inhabited continents joined by sport. The IOC does not tie any one colour to one continent.

probe.question: What do the five Olympic rings represent?
probe.wrong_answer: Five countries that founded the Games

misconceptions.root_belief: symbols mean what they first look like

misconceptions.statement: Olympic gold medals are made of solid gold.
misconceptions.why: The word 'gold medal' is taken to mean the medal is made of gold.
misconceptions.fix: Olympic gold medals are mostly silver with a thin coating of at least 6 grams of gold. Only the plating is gold.

probe.question: What is an Olympic gold medal mainly made of?

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: India's first Olympic medal was the hockey gold of 1928.
misconceptions.why: Hockey's golden era is the most celebrated part of India's Olympic story, so students assume it came first.
misconceptions.fix: The IOC credits Norman Pritchard with two silver medals in athletics at Paris 1900, India's first Olympic medals. The hockey gold came in 1928.

probe.question: In which sport did India win its first Olympic medals, and when?

misconceptions.root_belief: the most famous event was the first

misconceptions.statement: India's men's hockey team won gold at Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024.
misconceptions.why: The huge celebrations after ending a 41-year medal drought sound like a title win.
misconceptions.fix: India won bronze at both Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024. India's last hockey gold was at Moscow 1980.

probe.question: What medal did India's men's hockey team win at Paris 2024?

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger celebration means a higher prize

misconceptions.statement: Abhinav Bindra's gold at Beijing 2008 was India's first Olympic gold medal.
misconceptions.why: News called it a 'historic first gold', and students miss that it was the first individual one.
misconceptions.fix: India had already won eight gold medals in hockey. Bindra's 10 m air rifle gold in 2008 was India's first individual Olympic gold.

probe.question: How many Olympic gold medals had India won before 2008?

misconceptions.root_belief: first of a kind means first ever

misconceptions.statement: Neeraj Chopra won the gold medal in javelin at both Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024.
misconceptions.why: Students expect a champion to keep winning, and he remained the favourite in Paris.
misconceptions.fix: Neeraj won gold at Tokyo 2020 with 87.58 m. At Paris 2024 he won silver with 89.45 m, behind Arshad Nadeem's Olympic-record 92.97 m.

probe.question: What medal did Neeraj Chopra win at Paris 2024?

misconceptions.root_belief: a champion always keeps winning

misconceptions.statement: In javelin, the distance is measured from the place where the tail of the spear lands.
misconceptions.why: Students think the whole object must be measured to its far end.
misconceptions.fix: The throw is measured from the mark made by the tip of the javelin to the throwing arc. The tip must land first for the throw to count.

probe.question: A javelin lands with its tip at 80 m and its tail 2.6 m further back. What is the throw's distance?

misconceptions.root_belief: measure to the far end of the object

misconceptions.statement: PV Sindhu has won an Olympic gold medal in badminton.
misconceptions.why: She is India's most famous badminton player and won the 2019 World Championship gold, so students assume she also holds Olympic gold.
misconceptions.fix: Sindhu won silver at Rio 2016 and bronze at Tokyo 2020. Her gold came at the 2019 World Championships, which is not the Olympics.

probe.question: Which Olympic medals has PV Sindhu won?

misconceptions.root_belief: a world champion is also an Olympic champion

misconceptions.statement: PV Sindhu was the first Indian woman to win an Olympic medal.
misconceptions.why: Her fame in recent years hides the earlier women medallists.
misconceptions.fix: Karnam Malleswari won weightlifting bronze in 2000, and Saina Nehwal won badminton bronze in 2012. Sindhu was the first Indian woman to win two individual Olympic medals.

probe.question: Who was the first Indian woman to win an Olympic medal?

misconceptions.root_belief: the most famous person was the first

misconceptions.statement: The Paralympics and the Special Olympics are the same event.
misconceptions.why: Both involve athletes with disabilities and the names sound alike.
misconceptions.fix: The Paralympics are run by the International Paralympic Committee for elite athletes with impairments. Special Olympics is a separate organisation for people with intellectual disabilities.

probe.question: Are the Paralympics and the Special Olympics the same competition?

misconceptions.root_belief: similar names mean the same thing

misconceptions.statement: The Paralympics began in 1896 along with the first modern Olympics.
misconceptions.why: Students assume that two linked events began together.
misconceptions.fix: The Paralympic movement began in 1948 with a sports meet for injured war veterans at Stoke Mandeville, England. The first official Paralympics were held in Rome in 1960.

probe.question: In which year did the Paralympic movement begin?

misconceptions.root_belief: related events share the same start date

misconceptions.statement: Paralympic athletes are only people who use wheelchairs.
misconceptions.why: The wheelchair is the most common image of disability, so students treat it as the whole group.
misconceptions.fix: Paralympians include blind athletes, amputees, people with cerebral palsy, short stature or intellectual impairments, as well as wheelchair users.

probe.question: Can a blind runner compete in the Paralympics?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only wheelchair users take part

misconceptions.root_belief: one visible example stands for the whole group
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of children's and teachers' attitudes and ideas about disability and para-sport

misconceptions.statement: Paralympic sport is easier, so the standard is lower than in the Olympics.
misconceptions.why: Students think that different rules mean a lesser sport.
misconceptions.fix: Paralympians train as hard as Olympians and must meet qualifying standards. Classes group athletes with similar impairments so that skill decides the result.

probe.question: Do Paralympic athletes need to meet qualifying standards?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because the sports are easier

misconceptions.root_belief: different means lesser

misconceptions.statement: India started winning Paralympic medals only in recent years, with Tokyo 2020.
misconceptions.why: Media coverage of Paralympics grew only recently, so students assume India's success is new.
misconceptions.fix: Murlikant Petkar won India's first Paralympic gold, in swimming, in 1972. India won 19 medals at Tokyo 2020 and 29 at Paris 2024.

probe.question: When did India win its first Paralympic gold medal?

misconceptions.root_belief: recent attention means a recent beginning

misconceptions.statement: Doping means only injecting steroids.
misconceptions.why: Doping scandals in news often show needles and steroids.
misconceptions.fix: Doping covers many banned substances such as tablets, stimulants and masking agents. It also covers blood transfusion, tampering with tests and refusing a test.

probe.question: An athlete swallows a banned stimulant tablet. Is it doping?
probe.wrong_answer: No, doping is only injecting steroids

misconceptions.root_belief: one example is the whole category

misconceptions.statement: An athlete who took a banned substance without knowing it has not broken the doping rules.
misconceptions.why: In everyday life people are blamed less if they did something by accident.
misconceptions.fix: Under the anti-doping rule of strict liability, athletes are responsible for whatever is found in their body. Lack of intent may reduce the ban but does not remove the violation.

probe.question: A sprinter tests positive after a contaminated supplement and says she did not know. Has she broken the rules?
probe.wrong_answer: No, she did not know so she is innocent

misconceptions.root_belief: only intention decides whether you are guilty

misconceptions.statement: If a doctor prescribes a medicine, an athlete can use it in competition without any permission.
misconceptions.why: Students trust a doctor's authority and think a prescription makes any medicine allowed.
misconceptions.fix: Some prescribed medicines are on the banned list. The athlete must get a Therapeutic Use Exemption (TUE) before using them.

probe.question: A doctor prescribes a banned drug for an athlete. Can the athlete use it freely in competition?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because a doctor prescribed it

misconceptions.root_belief: approval from an authority makes anything allowed

misconceptions.statement: Each country makes its own list of banned substances, so rules differ from country to country.
misconceptions.why: Students know that laws differ between countries and assume sport rules do too.
misconceptions.fix: The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) publishes one Prohibited List used worldwide. In India, the National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA) follows it.

probe.question: Who decides which substances are banned for athletes worldwide?
probe.wrong_answer: Every country decides its own list

misconceptions.root_belief: every place has its own rules

misconceptions.statement: Doping tests are done only on the winners at the end of a competition.
misconceptions.why: Students see medal winners going for tests on television.
misconceptions.fix: Athletes can be tested at any time, in training or out of competition, and without notice. Some are chosen at random, not only winners.

probe.question: Can an athlete who finished last in an event be tested for doping?

misconceptions.root_belief: only the top performers are checked

misconceptions.statement: Fair play only means not taking banned drugs.
misconceptions.why: Doping is the most talked-about example of cheating, so it becomes the whole idea.
misconceptions.fix: Fair play also means following the rules, respecting opponents, officials and teammates, being honest, and accepting results gracefully.

probe.question: A player argues rudely with the referee but takes no drugs. Is that fair play?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, fair play is only about not taking drugs

misconceptions.root_belief: a single rule covers the whole of ethics

misconceptions.statement: The Olympic spirit says that the most important thing is to win.
misconceptions.why: The motto 'Faster, Higher, Stronger' and the medal table make winning seem like the only goal.
misconceptions.fix: The Olympic creed, linked to Pierre de Coubertin, says the important thing is not winning but taking part and doing one's best. The motto now ends with 'Together'.

probe.question: According to the Olympic creed, what is the most important thing in the Games?

misconceptions.root_belief: only the final result matters, not effort
